meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?
examples.trans: Wait, are you not listening to me at all?

examples.text: Или я для тебя пустое место?
examples.trans: Or am I invisible to you?
Vika, did you want to say something?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Am I talking to a wall?
What? Excuse me.
Vitya, what is going on here, pal?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('yes') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, nothing at all.
Oh, just family stuff.
It doesn't seem so.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You have to feed him so well.
Oh, just family stuff.

examples.text: Вы уж извините, что так вышло.
examples.trans: Please forgive me that it turned out this way.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'family', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: I discovered the secret of married life.
Oh, just family stuff.
It's a family holiday.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('I') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: I still work as a cook.
I finally proposed to Vika.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'already'.

examples.trans: Vika has really worn me out.
She has been asleep for a long time.
She has been my wife for half a year.

достать.gloss: to take out, to get, to reach

meanings.en: to take out, to get, to reach
meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (root 'стать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to take out', forming an aspectual pair with 'доставать'.

examples.trans: Vika has really worn me out.
I have had enough of this slave driver!
And take his eye out with a spoon.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'nag'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: She nags me over every little thing.
Keep at it, Kostya, keep at it.

examples.text: Юле бы дублёнку купили, Славику бы ноутбук.
examples.trans: We could have bought Yulia a sheepskin coat, and Slavik a laptop.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'along' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: I can see by your eyes that you don't understand.
She nags me over every little thing.
I'm here about the job.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'every', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: She nags me over every little thing.
Every day.
Every person.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'reason', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: She nags me over every little thing.
I'm calling about the shopping centre.
It's a good occasion.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to find', forming an aspectual pair with 'находить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Find some mistake of hers.
We will find someone else.
Well, we will find somebody.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('some') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Find some mistake of hers.
Put on some background noise.
Let's watch some film.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Find some mistake of hers.

examples.text: Тогда она не сможет тебя упрекнуть.
examples.trans: Then she won't be able to reproach you.
She is also a very famous chef.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'hers', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Find some mistake of hers.
What kind of mistake?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.

examples.text: Тогда она не сможет тебя упрекнуть.
examples.trans: Then she won't be able to reproach you.
Back then I was little.
Then come tomorrow.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('not') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?
examples.trans: Wait, are you not listening to me at all?
It does not matter.

examples.text: Тебе это на канал не пропустят.
examples.trans: They will not let that on television.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (root 'мочь'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to be able', forming an aspectual pair with 'мочь'.

examples.text: Тогда она не сможет тебя упрекнуть.
examples.trans: Then she won't be able to reproach you.
We came as soon as we could.
Will you be able to come tomorrow morning?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (root 'прекнуть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to reproach'.

examples.text: Тогда она не сможет тебя упрекнуть.
examples.trans: Then she won't be able to reproach you.
Oh, just family stuff.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('what') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: What kind of mistake?
What is your town like?
What a beautiful house!

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to know'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Знаете, боюсь, мне это не грозит.
examples.trans: You know, I am afraid that is not a threat for me.
I don't know.
Well, I don't know, Max.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'or', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Или я для тебя пустое место?
examples.trans: Or am I invisible to you?
Or maybe she uses your razor.

examples.text: А ты обследование прошла или нет?
examples.trans: Wait, did you take your medical check-up or not?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'razor', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Or maybe she uses your razor.
Take my razor.

examples.text: У меня с собой даже бритвы нет.
examples.trans: I don't even have a razor with me.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: Or maybe she uses your razor.
We will feed your guests properly right away.
This is your coffee.

пользоваться.gloss: to use, to take advantage of

meanings.en: to use, to take advantage of
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (root 'льзоваться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to use', forming an aspectual pair with 'воспользоваться'.

examples.trans: Or maybe she uses your razor.
You're taking advantage of my weakness!
Of course I am.

бывать.gloss: to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit

meanings.en: to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to happen', forming an aspectual pair with 'быть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Does that really happen?

examples.text: У мужчины бывает не только жена.
examples.trans: A man can have more than just a wife.
That happens.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('but') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Does that really happen?

examples.text: Я же сказал, договорюсь с Нагиевым.
examples.trans: I told you, I will make a deal with Nagiyev.

examples.text: Я же тебя просила не бриться моим станком.
examples.trans: I asked you not to shave with my razor.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('such') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Does that really happen?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('seemingly') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It doesn't seem so.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('no') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, nothing at all.

meanings.note: Prefix 'ис-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (root 'кать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to look for'.

examples.trans: I'm looking for a job.

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
